summary:
Mpumalanga is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position on consensual conduct, the gender-recognition statute, the hate-crime provisions and the national correctional rulings are carried by the national record. The findings below are those specific to the province.

Traditional-authority structures have been openly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships. A published letter of June 2010, issued by the National House of Traditional Leaders together with its provincial houses after a meeting held at Hazyview in Mpumalanga, stated that traditional leaders were disappointed that the Constitutional Court's marriage judgment had given what the letter called an immoral practice a lifeline, declared that they did not support legalisation of same-sex marriage, warned of ostracism and violence, and committed to a five-year campaign against it. The same structure asked Parliament in 2016 to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Violence against people read as sexuality- or gender-nonconforming has produced both a killing and a mass response inside the province. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, in Thembisile Hani Local Municipality, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019; she was half naked and had stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the same municipality in protest, in a demonstration organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence.

Public LGBTIQ+ presence has also drawn official cooperation. Mpumalanga's first Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital, then Nelspruit and now Mbombela, under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United'. Around 1,000 participants marched from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza, followed by a picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. The organiser, Joy Kunene, said police were visible and supportive and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers; the event launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella body for the province's LGBTI organisations.

Police conduct is the most consistently reported grievance. At a Pride Flag Tour event held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August 2026, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after she was sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she had not fought back. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation.

The documented pattern is community-level violence and police mistreatment inside a protective national legal framework. Enforcement appears to turn on the individual station, municipality or venue rather than on any province-wide practice, and the sources identify no Mpumalanga-specific court ruling, provincial policy or facilities rule.
tangentialFactors:
The province's record runs in two directions. In 2014 the police presence at the capital's first Pride was described by the organiser as visible and supportive, with roughly 20 police and traffic officers supplied; in 2026 community members in eMbalenhle described being ridiculed and questioned at police stations, including by an officer responding to a sexual-assault report. Both accounts come from the province and neither cancels the other.

Documented incidents cluster in particular municipalities rather than spreading evenly. The 2019 killing and the 2020 march fall in Thembisile Hani Local Municipality, and the 2026 complaints fall in the eMbalenhle area of Govan Mbeki Local Municipality. The sources record nothing comparable for the provincial capital or for other districts, which may reflect reporting density as much as the distribution of risk.

The province's named LGBTIQ+ organisational infrastructure is small: the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, launched in 2014 as an umbrella for the province's organisations, Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, which organised the 2020 march, and the Rainbow Seed Institute, which led the 2026 event. National organisations and national litigation carry the weight of the legal work.
localsOnly:
Residents rather than visitors absorb the enforcement record. The grievances raised at the eMbalenhle event concerned ordinary dealings with police stations and other government offices, and attendees said the fear of stigmatisation deters them from reporting crimes at all, which leaves assaults and discrimination unreported and unrecorded.

Local mobilisation has been the main response to violence. The march in Thembisile Hani in January 2020 followed the killing of a resident of the municipality and was organised by a local LGBTI organisation together with the ANC Women's League and others, with the municipal mayor publicly calling on parents, leaders and churches to oppose gender-based violence.

In rural parts of the province under traditional authority, the 2010 position of the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses, issued after a meeting at Hazyview, and the five-year campaign it announced, describe the local power structure a resident may have to deal with. The sources record no later provincial statement from that structure.
outOfScopeNotes:
No outcome is sourced for the investigation into the December 2019 killing of Portia Mtsweni, and no arrest, prosecution or conviction is recorded.

No disciplinary, criminal or other follow-up is sourced for the allegation that an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station questioned a sexual-assault complainant about why she had not fought back, or for the wider complaints of discrimination at government offices raised in August 2026.

No Mpumalanga-specific prosecution data under the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act is available in the sources, and no provincial hate-crime or Equality Court case from the province is identified.

No provincial policy on facilities access, and no provincial health-department statement on gender-affirming care or waiting times, appears in the sources. Whether the 2010 traditional-leadership campaign continued past the five years it announced is unresolved.

No province-level statistics on violence against transgender people are available; the violence material for Mpumalanga consists of individual incidents, which carry no rate and cannot be compared with the province's general homicide figures.
